name: Barkcloth making in Uganda
date_note: Practice ancient among the Baganda; proclaimed 2005, inscribed 2008
making_significance: Baganda craftspeople strip mutuba (Ficus natalensis) bark and beat it into cloth for royal dress, burial and ceremony.
materials_techniques: Ficus natalensis bark; mallets; steaming; beating

free_sources: UNESCO ICH lists (link out; per-item photo licence); Wikimedia Commons; community-published site

date_note: Asante tradition dates silk kente to the 17th–18th century; Ewe weaving older by some accounts
making_significance: Asante and Ewe weavers make narrow strips on the treadle loom and sew them into patterned cloths whose designs carry names and proverbs.

name: Aso oke weaving

materials_techniques: narrow treadle loom; cotton; silk; lurex

free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); British Museum collection online (link out); Wikimedia Commons; community-published site

materials_techniques: handwoven cotton strips; n'gallama leaf dye; fermented mud; soap bleaching
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons; community-published site
notes: Industrial "mud cloth" prints are a copying case.

date_note: Adire on imported shirting from the late 19th century
making_significance: Yoruba women resist-dye cotton in indigo using cassava-starch paste, raffia ties and stitches.

free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); British Museum collection online (link out); Wikimedia Commons; community-published site

name: Kuba raffia textile making
date_note: Collected from the 17th century; practice older
making_significance: Kuba men weave raffia squares and women embroider cut-pile and appliqué patterns that are worn, exchanged and buried with the dead.

free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons; community-published site

name: Ceebu jën, a culinary art of Senegal
